newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-Do the NZ Coalition's fiscal plans add up?.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Do the NZ Coalition's fiscal plans add up?.

text.p: By David Plank, Chief Economist Bankers Trust NZ
AUCKLAND, Dec 18 - New Zealand's new era of coalition government was ushered in last week after seven weeks of negotiations.

While there has been much comment about the "$5 billion" in extra spending planned by the new government, there has been little focus on whether the ambitious policy programme can be fitted within this cap.

Our analysis suggests it will be difficult, if not impossible -- unless the costings set out in the agreement are too high, some of the policies are not implemented, and/or savings are made from other areas of government expenditure.
The coalition document runs to more than 70 pages. The document sets out:
* the "fundamental principles" of the new government;
* the split of the Cabinet between National and NZ First;
* dispute resolution procedures;
* the policies agreed by the partners to the coalition (in varying degrees of detail); and
* the fiscal parameters within which the coalition government agrees to operate.
In numerous places the agreement states that "all funding proposals (are) subject to being considered within the agreed spending policy parameters".

Further, the coalition partners agreed "that a budgetary programme prioritising expenditure will be prepared with the consent of both parties, such programme being within the fiscal parameters as set out" in the agreement.

These statements imply a commitment on the part of both coalition partners to contain the increases in expenditure within the set limits. An analysis of the policy programme within the document reveals this will be no mean feat.

The following table sets out the spending limits prescribed in the agreement and then deducts the policies that are actually costed to give the amount left over for those policies which aren't costed (or, as we now know, which weren't included in the original agreement).
In creating the table, we've had to make a number of assumptions:
* Unless otherwise specified, all policies are assumed to
begin in the 1997/98 fiscal year;
* the $30 million over three years for organic farming
research has been divided equally into each year and
possum control research is assumed to cost $3.75 million
per annum more than current baselines;
* employment policy is assumed to cost nothing above current
baselines in 1999/2000. The document specifies a cost of
$80 million in 1998/1999, so this assumption may not be
realistic. If the employment programmes have a similar
cost in 1999/2000, then the sum of identified costs for
that year will be above the $2100 million cap;
* the lower bound of National's estimate is used for the
cost of law and order policy;
* no allowance is made for funding of women's issues as the

programmes in this year).
On top of this, the list of uncosted policies is significant. This list includes:
* the abolition of the surcharge from 1 April 1998 (before
the changes under the National/United coalition, which
cost around $100 million, the surcharge raised about $300
million per annum);
* Maori policy;
* Defence (the need for more funding is acknowledged in the document);
* Justice;
* Tourism;
* Transport;
* policies which were not included in the document released last week.

Our analysis shows there is little room to fund these "uncosted" policies within the agreed spending cap, especially once the cost of abolishing the surcharge is considered, unless the costings in the coalition agreement are too high.
Bankers Trust is not in a position to check the accuracy of those costings.
There are a number of options available to the coalition government to create some headroom. These might include:
* Reducing the scope or delaying the implementation of some
policies.
The government could choose not to proceed in some areas
given the fiscal constraints.
Another option is to delay implementation. In many policy
areas there is no commitment on the time-frame for
proceeding. This allows the government to prioritise its
policy commitments and proceed with those deemed most
important. This is the option the coalition agreement
refers to.
It is also worth pointing out that many policies will
require more work before they can be implemented. Thus,
the assumption that all policies will begin in the 1997/98
fiscal year is unrealistic.
However, if the intention is to introduce policies by the
beginning of the 1999/2000 fiscal year at the latest, then
fitting within the cap remains difficult (if not
impossible once the cost of the surcharge abolition is
included)
* Increasing the cap.
The coalition agreement specifies a spending limit above
DEFU baselines of $2100 million (excluding additional
financing costs) by 1999/2000.
The easy way out for the government would be to simply
increase the amount it is prepared to spend. However, this
will further increase the tension between monetary and
fiscal policy and could impose a high cost on the export
sector. It would also raise serious concerns about the
"fiscal" credibility of the coalition.
* Raiding the contingency expense provision.
The fiscal projections include $200 million in each year
set aside as a contingency expense provision. This could
be reduced and so "free-up" more money to spend.
However, this would quickly be seen for the "smoke and
mirrors" trick it is. The provision is there to provide a
cushion for the government's projected surplus.
There are a large number of fiscal risks facing the
government which can hit at any time. Reducing the
contingency provision cannot be considered a saving.
* Looking for savings elsewhere.
There may be low priority areas where the government could
make savings. This would allow higher priority spending to
take place without placing pressure on the cap.
This analysis suggests the 1997 budget round could be difficult.

It is rare that a budget round produces less spending (or greater savings) than was intended at the start of the process. The spending plans outlined in the coalition agreement have raised expectations in a large number of areas.
At least some of these expectations look likely to be disappointed if the coalition government wishes to remain true to its fiscal plans.

There must be a real concern that the spending plans in each year represent a starting point which will soon be exceeded. Budget expenditure has a habit of ratcheting up each year as baselines are added to.

The Budget Policy Statement (due the end of March) will provide at least some of the answers as to how the government will proceed with the task ahead. For the time being, the market's cautious reaction to the coalition agreement, which has seen the yield curve become less inverted (a sign that higher inflation is being priced in) seems appropriate.
